mcqs.question: Why does a Huffman code never need a delimiter between encoded symbols?
options: Because every code word in a Huffman code always has the same length
Because a prefix-free code guarantees no code word is a prefix of another, so a decoder always knows exactly when one symbol's code ends and the next begins
Because Huffman codes always use exactly two bits per symbol
Because the decoder always knows the total message length in advance
mcqs.explanation: The correct reasoning is prefix-freeness, not fixed length (Huffman codes are explicitly variable-length). Since no complete code word is ever a prefix of another, a decoder reading bit by bit always recognizes the exact moment a valid code word is complete, with no separator needed.

mcqs.question: The Huffman exchange argument claims the two rarest symbols can always be placed at the deepest level of some optimal tree. What makes the swap that proves this safe?
options: Swapping only works when all frequencies happen to be equal

Placing the smallest frequencies at the deepest (longest-code) positions and moving whatever was there to a shallower position can only decrease or maintain the total weighted code length, since a large frequency times a short depth plus a small frequency times a long depth beats the reverse pairing
The rarest symbols must always end up as direct children of the root
The swap increases total code length but simplifies the tree's structure
mcqs.explanation: This is the crux of the exchange argument: total weighted code length is minimized by pairing large frequencies with short depths and small frequencies with long depths, so moving the rarest symbols to the deepest positions (and displacing whatever occupied them) can never make the total worse.

mcqs.question: When does Huffman coding offer little to no advantage over a simple fixed-length code?
options: When the number of distinct symbols is a power of two
When the symbol frequency distribution is close to uniform, since Huffman's tree ends up nearly balanced and its code lengths converge toward what fixed-length coding already gives
Huffman coding always outperforms fixed-length coding regardless of frequency distribution
When the alphabet contains fewer than 10 symbols
mcqs.explanation: Huffman's savings come specifically from assigning shorter codes to more frequent symbols — with a near-uniform distribution there's little frequency skew to exploit, so the resulting tree is close to balanced and offers minimal improvement over fixed-length codes.

mcqs.question: Why is Huffman tree construction O(n log n) rather than O(n²)?
options: Because a min-heap makes each 'find the two smallest remaining' operation O(log n) instead of the O(n) a linear scan would require, across n-1 merge rounds
Because the algorithm only processes half of the symbols
Because Huffman coding sorts the input only once at the very start
Because merging two nodes is an O(log n) operation by itself
mcqs.explanation: The heap is what makes this efficient — without it, repeatedly finding the two smallest remaining weights via linear scan would cost O(n) per round across n-1 rounds, giving O(n²) total. The heap operations (pop, pop, push) are each O(log n), and the merge itself (summing two weights) is O(1).

mcqs.question: Two symbols tie in frequency during Huffman tree construction, and choosing which pair to merge first produces a different tree with different code words. What does this tell you?
options: Multiple optimal trees can exist with the same total weighted code length — the tie affects which specific tree you get, not whether the result is optimal
The algorithm has a bug and needs a tie-breaking fix to be correct
The total weighted code length will differ depending on which pair is merged first
Ties are impossible in a correctly implemented Huffman algorithm
mcqs.explanation: Huffman's guarantee is about the total weighted code length being optimal, not about producing one unique tree — ties genuinely can produce different, equally-optimal trees. Requiring one specific tree shape is a separate, additional constraint (usually a tie-breaking convention) beyond what the algorithm itself guarantees.
